These 3 habits are the difference. Save this for your next revision session.

slides.title:
Here are ((3 habits))
that turn past papers
into actual marks
slides.kicker: the second one hurts a little.

slides.title:
Go by topic before
you go full paper.
slides.body: A full paper tests 20 topics at once, so you never see the pattern. Do one chapter's questions back to back until it clicks. *Then* sit full papers.

slides.title:
Mark it like the
examiner. *Strictly.*
slides.body: No “I basically had it”. If the mark scheme wants the unit, the unit *is* the mark. Be meaner than the examiner and the real thing feels easy.

slides.title: Keep a ((mistakes page)).
slides.body: Every lost mark goes on one page: the question, what you wrote, what they wanted. Read it before every paper. It becomes your most valuable notes.
slides.try: same mistake twice → top of the list.

posts.caption:
The mark scheme is literally the examiner's brain on paper. 🧠

Once you can read it, you know exactly where your marks went (and how to stop losing them).

M1, A1, B1, ft, oe, cao: decoded. Save this one.

slides.title:
Mark scheme codes,
==decoded.==
items: **Method mark.** Right method, even if the arithmetic goes wrong later.
**Accuracy mark.** Correct answer, but only if you earned the M mark first.
**Independent mark.** A correct fact or value on its own.
**Follow through.** Your earlier wrong answer, used correctly, still scores.
**Or equivalent.** 0.5, ½ and 50% can all be right.
**Correct answer only.** No partial credit. Exact, or nothing.
slides.tail: moral: always show your method. M1 is free marks.

Your brain remembers what it has to *retrieve*, not what it re-reads. Close the book and answer questions.

slides.title:
Stop ~~highlighting~~.
Start ((answering)).
slides.sub: Re-reading feels productive. Your brain only remembers what it has to *pull back out*. Questions do that. Highlighters don't.
slides.note: **Try it tonight:** close the book. Write down everything you remember about one topic. *Then* check what you missed.
